title: 2-minute English documentary with numbers, places, names and a list
scenes: In 1969 the United States spent about 25.4 billion dollars to put two men on the Moon.
Mission control in Houston followed every second while 400,000 people worked on the project.
Dr. Margaret Hamilton wrote the flight software that kept the computers from crashing.
Here are three reasons the landing succeeded. First, careful testing. Second, a brave crew. Third, steady leadership.
The spacecraft left Florida on July 16 and travelled 384,000 kilometres to the Moon.
Neil Armstrong said: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."
Back on Earth, about 600 million people watched from Tokyo, London, Cairo and Karachi.
In Japan the broadcast reached nearly 95 percent of homes with a television set.
Costs were huge, yet the programme created thousands of new inventions and jobs.
Prices of computer chips fell 50 percent within five years because of the demand.
Russia had launched the first satellite in 1957, which started the space race.
By 1972 the American programme had sent twelve people to walk on the surface.
Today India, China and Europe also plan missions, and the budget is much smaller than in 1969.
The sea of Tranquility stayed quiet, and the footprints are still there without any wind.
Engineers compare the old computers with a phone, which is millions of times faster.
The crew landed with only about 25 seconds of fuel left, a risk few people knew about.
Scientists later brought back 382 kilograms of rock that taught us how the Moon formed.
Many countries signed a treaty in 1967 that keeps space open for peaceful use.
Now private companies in America and Europe want to return before 2030.
The story shows what a nation can do when it chooses one clear goal and works together.
